title: Deployment and Release Management: Canary, Blue-Green, Rolling
bodyMarkdown:
## Why Release Strategy Matters

Most outages are triggered by **change**. Operationally excellent teams make releases **progressive, observable, and reversible** to shrink blast radius and recovery time. The PCA exam expects you to map a scenario's constraints (downtime tolerance, rollback speed, mixed-version safety, traffic-shaping needs) to the right strategy.

## The Core Strategies

| Strategy | How it works | Pros | Cons / constraints |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rolling update** | Replace instances/pods in batches | No downtime, simple, cheap | Old + new run together; slower rollback |
| **Blue-green** | Two full environments; atomic switch | Instant rollback; no mixed versions in flight | Double resources; DB migration care |
| **Canary** | Small traffic slice to new version, then promote | Smallest blast radius; data-driven | Needs traffic shaping + good metrics |
| **Recreate** | Stop old, start new | Simplest | Causes downtime |
| **A/B testing** | Route cohorts to variants | Product experimentation | Not a safety/rollback mechanism |

## Rolling Updates on Google Cloud

For a **managed instance group (MIG)**, a rolling update applies a new **instance template** with controls:

- **maxSurge**: extra instances allowed above target during the update.
- **maxUnavailable**: how many instances may be down at once.

Set maxUnavailable to 0 and maxSurge > 0 for true zero-downtime. MIGs also support a **canary** by updating only a portion of instances to the new template.

On **GKE**, a Deployment defaults to a `RollingUpdate` strategy with its own maxSurge/maxUnavailable, while `Recreate` causes downtime.

## Blue-Green on Google Cloud

Deploy the new ('green') environment in parallel, validate it, then **switch traffic atomically** by repointing the load balancer backend service or DNS. Keep 'blue' warm so rollback is a switch back. Choose blue-green when you need **near-instant rollback** and **no two versions serving simultaneously** (e.g., strict schema constraints). Watch out for **database migrations**: prefer backward/forward-compatible (expand-contract) schema changes so both versions can run during the transition if needed.

## Canary on Google Cloud

Canary sends a **small percentage** of live traffic to the new version, observes golden signals/SLOs, then promotes in stages.

**Cloud Deploy** is the managed continuous-delivery service that orchestrates this:

- Define a **delivery pipeline** with ordered targets (dev -> staging -> prod).
- Use a **canary deployment strategy** with configurable traffic percentages (e.g., 5% -> 25% -> 100%).
- Add **automated verification** steps and gate promotion on health; configure **automatic rollback** on failure.
- Get auditable promotions and approvals.

For GKE/Cloud Run, traffic splitting is native (Cloud Run revisions support percentage splits; GKE via Gateway/Service Mesh).

## Decision Guide

- Need **zero downtime, cheap, simple**, mixed versions acceptable -> **rolling**.
- Need **instant rollback** and **no mixed versions** -> **blue-green**.
- Need **smallest blast radius** with metric-gated promotion -> **canary** (Cloud Deploy).
- Need **product experiment** on user cohorts -> **A/B** (not a release-safety tool).

Always pair any strategy with monitoring and a tested rollback.
